title: Declining the Louis Armstrong All Stars at $450 a week
summary: Armstrong's road manager would not pay the $450 Callender asked, so Arvell Shaw took the job and Callender went to Honolulu.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: 1947. And it was right after this that Joe Glaser decided to puts Pops in front of a small group. So he got Jack Teagarden and Barney Bigard... I don't know whether Zutty was doing that at this time or not.
When I saw the group, it was two years later. Big Sid was the drummer.

Uh-huh. Anyhow, when it first got off the ground, they called me, and I had just finished doing the picture, you know, making some very nice bread. Because I was working independently, I had my own agent. So Frenchy, who was Pops'...

...road manager, called me and said, "Hey, we're going to start to work in a couple of weeks." So I said, "Wait a minute. How much money are you talking about?" So he said, "What do you want?" So I said, "Well, I figure I'm worth 450 bucks a week at least." So he said,
"What? For a bass player?" So he said, "We can't pay that kind of money." So I said, "Well, you don't need me."
Well, that's the way I felt. So they got Arvell...
Arvell Shaw took the job. I guess he felt differently than I did.
Well, he was just sort of starting out. He wasn't established like you were at the time. I mean, Arvell was practically a teenager when he started with Louis.

Anyhow, he took the job. And I figured if I'm going to play "Sleepy Time Down South" every night for the next five years, they are going to have to pay me! So it didn't bother me at all that they didn't want to pay $450 a week, which was really nothing. They made up to $25,000 a night for that aggregation. What was $450 a week? Nothing! So anyhow, I didn't take it, and it was shortly after that I went off to Honolulu (and I covered part of that already) and got my own band together, and played in the symphony.
